outline.section: H2: What Happens to Your Skin as You Age?
outline.guidance: Explain the three core biological shifts that make aging skin behave differently: (1) collagen and elastin production slows, leading to loss of firmness; (2) the skin barrier weakens as ceramide levels drop, causing transepidermal water loss (TEWL) and chronic dryness; (3) cell turnover slows, so dead skin accumulates and skin looks dull. Mention that these changes often first show up on the body — arms, legs, neck, décolletage — not just the face. Keep it accessible, not clinical. Cite a credible source (e.g., AAD or peer-reviewed dermatology journal) for the collagen decline statistic. This section justifies everything that follows and establishes E-E-A-T.

outline.section: H2: Key Ingredients to Look for in a Body Lotion for Aging Skin
outline.guidance: This is the 'what to look for on the label' section — make it scannable with a short intro paragraph followed by a bulleted or bolded list of 6–7 ingredients with a 2–3 sentence explanation for each. Cover: (1) Coconut oil — occlusive, rich in fatty acids, helps seal in moisture and soften dry, rough skin; (2) Hyaluronic acid — humectant, draws water into skin; (3) Ceramides — restore the lipid barrier; (4) Shea butter or plant-based butters — emollient, softens and soothes; (5) Glycerin — humectant, widely recommended for dry aging skin; (6) Antioxidants (vitamin C, vitamin E, green tea extract) — combat free radical damage that accelerates skin aging; (7) Peptides or plant-based firming actives — support collagen-adjacent skin structure. Do NOT recommend retinol as a 'must-have' (it positions this post against clean-ingredient values); you may briefly note that some people use retinol body lotions but that there are effective clean alternatives. Do not name competitor brands. Cite the AAD or a dermatology source for at least one ingredient claim.

outline.section: H2: Ingredients to Avoid in a Body Lotion for Aging Skin
outline.guidance: Short but important section that helps readers filter out products — this is a clean-brand differentiator. Cover: (1) Parabens — potential endocrine disruptors, cite EWG or a peer-reviewed source; (2) Synthetic fragrance — a leading cause of contact dermatitis, especially in mature, sensitive skin; (3) Mineral oil and petrolatum — occlusive but potentially pore-clogging and not skin-nourishing; (4) Alcohol denat. — strips the skin barrier, worsens dryness. Frame this as empowering the reader to read labels, not as fear-mongering. Naturally weave in 'paraben free lotion' and 'all natural coconut oil body lotion' concepts without keyword stuffing.

e_e_a_t_signals: Cite at least two authoritative external sources (AAD, NCBI/PubMed, or a dermatology organization) for biological claims about skin aging — collagen decline statistics, TEWL, ceramide function

Frame ingredient recommendations around peer-reviewed or clinically observed efficacy, not marketing language — e.g., 'glycerin has been shown in multiple studies to improve skin hydration' with a citation

Include a brief author bio note or reviewer credential line at the top or bottom of the post (e.g., 'Reviewed by a licensed esthetician' or 'Written by the Real Skin Care editorial team with input from skincare specialists')

Acknowledge nuance: note that results vary by individual skin type and that very dry or medical skin conditions (like eczema) may warrant a dermatologist visit — this builds trust by not overpromising
Use specific, verifiable ingredient claims rather than vague adjectives — 'coconut oil contains lauric acid, a medium-chain fatty acid that penetrates skin' rather than 'deeply nourishes'
Add a 'Last Updated' date to the post and commit to reviewing it annually — signals freshness and editorial responsibility
citation_guidance: The following claims require outbound citations to credible sources: (1) Statistics on collagen production decline with age — cite AAD (aad.org) or a peer-reviewed dermatology journal (e.g., Journal of Investigative Dermatology); (2) Claims about transepidermal water loss (TEWL) increasing with age — cite a dermatology or cosmetic science source; (3) Ceramide function in the skin barrier — cite AAD or NCBI; (4) Efficacy of glycerin as a humectant — cite a published study or AAD guidelines; (5) Parabens as potential endocrine disruptors — cite EWG or an EPA/NIH source, but soften to 'potential concerns' rather than absolute safety claims since the research is not definitive; (6) Coconut oil as an emollient with lauric acid — cite a cosmetic dermatology source or peer-reviewed paper. Do NOT make absolute claims like 'X ingredient cures aging skin' or 'Y chemical causes cancer' — soften all safety/efficacy language to 'may help,' 'has been shown to,' or 'dermatologists often recommend.' Avoid citing any brand websites as authoritative sources on ingredient science.
writer_notes: Tone: warm, knowledgeable, and direct — like advice from a trusted friend who happens to know a lot about skincare. Avoid fear-mongering about aging. Frame aging skin as a natural, manageable change — not a problem to be fixed. Do NOT use the word 'anti-aging' in the title or H1 (the brand leans toward positive, empowering language about mature skin); it can appear naturally in body copy. Do NOT name competitor brands anywhere in the post. The listicle items (H2: 1 through H2: 5) describe lotion FORMATS and ingredient profiles, not specific third-party brands — this is intentional to keep the post evergreen and brand-safe. Real Skin Care's own product is the only named brand featured. Keep sentences short and paragraphs to 3–4 lines max for readability on mobile. Avoid keyword stuffing — if a phrase sounds unnatural, rephrase it. Do not pad sections to hit word counts — every sentence should earn its place. Watch the historical flops: previous posts on 'organic body lotion,' 'natural lotion,' and 'clean body lotion' failed due to intent mismatch — this post succeeds because it squarely matches commercial listicle intent. Do not drift into vague 'natural is better' messaging without grounding it in specific ingredient benefits.
